opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and honestly one we're still figuring out. Right now the model tends to spend a fairly consistent amount of time on most requests, and I think that's not ideal. Some questions genuinely need ten or twenty minutes of digging through lots of sources, cross-referencing, and backtracking when something doesn't add up. Others, frankly, you could answer well in a minute or two, and making someone wait longer isn't a better experience.

So ideally the model learns to calibrate based on the request itself. How ambiguous is it? How many distinct pieces of information does it need to pull together? Is this something where the answer is spread across a lot of obscure sources, or is it relatively well-documented? A human researcher does this intuitively. If your manager asks you a quick factual question, you don't go off for a week. But if they ask for a full market analysis, you know you need to go deep.

Part of it is also on the user side. Clarifying questions at the start help a lot, because they tighten the scope before the model commits to a long search. And I think over time we'd like users to be able to signal how much effort they want, whether that's "give me a quick overview" or "be really exhaustive here."

The bigger picture is that we want the model to stop when it's actually confident it has a good answer, not when it hits some fixed budget. Training it to recognize that point, and not to overthink or underthink, is a big part of making these agents feel genuinely useful rather than just slow and thorough by default.

r001.rationale: It says the model should learn to calibrate its effort to the request and stop when confident, while presenting user effort signals as an additional input.

r002.rationale: It describes a fairly consistent amount of time spent on most requests, but does not say Deep Research always uses maximum thinking time or identify that policy as the cause of frustrating delays.

r003.rationale: It mentions user-selectable quick or exhaustive effort, but makes no prediction about o3 or a successor offering an intermediate option below Deep Research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot. The honest answer is that we don't think there's a single right amount of time, because it really depends on the question. If someone asks what the capital of France is, spending twenty minutes browsing the web and reading fifty sources is actually a worse experience, not a better one. But if someone asks for a comparison of every mid-size SUV with a specific set of constraints, or a literature review on some niche area, then five minutes is probably not enough and the user would rather wait.

So the ideal is that the model itself learns to calibrate. One of the nice things about training with reinforcement learning on these browsing tasks is that the model gets rewarded for actually finding the right answer, and part of what it picks up is when to keep going and when it has enough. If it opens a few sources and they all agree and the question was simple, it should stop. If it keeps finding contradictory information, or it realizes there are sub-questions it hasn't resolved, it should keep searching. We see this behavior emerge to some degree, where the model will backtrack, try a different query, or decide it needs to dig into a particular source more deeply.

That said, we also think the user should have some input. Deep Research right now does the clarifying questions step at the beginning, and part of the point of that is to understand how thorough someone wants this to be and what they actually care about. Someone who's doing a quick sanity check wants something different from someone who's making a big purchasing decision or writing a report for work. We'd rather spend a little effort up front understanding that than spend thirty minutes producing something that answers the wrong question.

And then over time I think the product will just get better at this. Today it's somewhat blunt, and it can take longer than it needs to on some things. But the direction we want to go is one where the amount of compute spent scales naturally with the difficulty and the stakes of the task, and the user basically doesn't have to think about it.

r001.rationale: The response says the ideal is for the model to learn to calibrate how long to search based on the question, while treating user input as an additional factor.

r002.rationale: It says excessive research can make simple queries worse and that Deep Research can take longer than needed, but does not identify a policy of always using maximum thinking time as the cause.

r003.rationale: It does not predict an o3 or successor option for an intermediate thinking time below Deep Research.

astra-6.text:
I think it should depend on what the user is trying to accomplish. If you’re asking a fairly straightforward question, you probably don’t want to wait ten minutes for an answer. But if you’re asking for a detailed report that would otherwise take you hours to put together, spending more time can be worthwhile.

The tricky part is figuring out when that extra time is actually improving the answer. Is there an important gap we still need to investigate? Are there conflicting sources we need to reconcile? Or are we just continuing to search without learning much more?

So I’d want it to infer a reasonable amount of effort from the request, but also let the user steer that. You should be able to say, “I need a quick answer,” or, “Take your time and be thorough.” And it should know when it has enough information to give you something useful.

r001.rationale: The response says the system should infer a reasonable effort, but also says users should be able to steer it; it does not argue that the model should decide instead of the user.

r002.rationale: It says straightforward questions should not require a ten-minute wait, but does not identify Deep Research’s policy of always using maximum thinking time as the cause.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction about o3 or a successor offering an intermediate thinking-time option.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should depend on what the user is trying to accomplish. If you want a quick overview, you probably don’t want to wait ten minutes. If you’re making an important decision and need a thorough report, spending more time could be worthwhile.

The hard part is that the system has to make that judgment before it knows everything the research will uncover. So it should start with an estimate of how much work the task needs, then adjust as it goes. Are we still finding information that could change the answer? Are there unresolved questions that actually matter to the user?

And I think users should have some control over that tradeoff. You should be able to say, “Give me what you have now,” or, “Take more time and go deeper.” The goal isn’t to think for as long as possible. It’s to spend time where it makes the result more useful.

r001.rationale: It says the system should estimate the work required and adjust as it proceeds, so it assigns the thinking-time decision to the model while also allowing user input.

r002.rationale: It notes that a quick overview should not require a long wait, but does not identify an always-maximum-thinking policy as the cause of frustrating delays.

r003.rationale: It does not mention o3, a successor, or an intermediate thinking-time option below Deep Research.
